report:
## What the Evidence Shows

The claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism is not supported by scientific evidence — and this conclusion rests on a large, consistent body of research spanning decades and countries.

**Origins of the claim:** The vaccine-autism link traces to a 1998 Lancet paper by Andrew Wakefield linking the MMR vaccine to autism. That paper was later found to be fraudulent, was retracted, and Wakefield lost his medical license (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Wakefield). This scandal is widely cited as the root of the modern anti-vaccine movement.

**"Too many, too soon" specifically:** This is a distinct hypothesis from MMR-specific claims — that cumulative vaccine numbers or timing overwhelm a child's system. The Institute of Medicine (National Academy of Sciences) reviewed this question and found no evidence supporting a causal relationship between the immunization schedule and autism (shotofprevention.com/2013/03/29/study-concludes-concern-over-too-many-too-soon-is-unfounded/).

**Large-scale data:** A 2014 meta-analysis pooling over 1.2 million children (5 cohort + 5 case-control studies) found no association between vaccination — including MMR or thimerosal exposure — and autism (sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X14006367). A 2025 Danish study of 1.2 million children similarly found no link between aluminum-containing vaccines and autism, even at high cumulative doses (nytimes.com/interactive/2025/08/19/opinion/vaccines-autism-evidence.html). In December 2025, a WHO expert committee reaffirmed no causal link exists between vaccines and autism (who.int/news/item/11-12-2025-who-expert-group-s-new-analysis-reaffirms-there-is-no-link-between-vaccines-and-autism).

**Recent political controversy:** In November 2025, CDC — under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine skeptic — altered its website language to cast doubt on this consensus. Fact-checkers noted this change was not evidence-based and reflected political rather than scientific input (factcheck.org/2025/11/revised-cdc-website-about-autism-and-vaccines-is-not-evidence-based/).

**Bottom line:** The scientific consensus, based on millions of children studied across multiple countries, is that vaccines and vaccine schedules do not cause autism.
